Issued at 400 PM CDT Mon Sep 28 2026

The morning fog (a rare pure radiational fog to impact the core of 
the Twin Cities urban heat island) has burned off, but as seen with 
the 12z MPX sounding, the low level moisture that led to the fog is 
trapped beneath a stout inversion around h85, which means that fog 
simply lifted into the stratocu field we have. This low level 
moisture trapped beneath an inversion setup will continue through 
tonight, which means a mostly cloud night, though with enough wind 
to keep us from getting fog. Rain tonight will be confined to the 
north of the wavy frontal boundary that this afternoon sits from 
roughly Fargo to Duluth and then back west in the Dakotas along an 
eastward advancing cold front.

For Tuesday and Wednesday, there are two features to watch, a short 
wave currently over western Montana and the combination of the upper 
low near Las Vegas and Hurricane Polo approaching the Baja Peninsula 
of Mexico. Overall, we've seen a significant downward trend in 
precipitation potential across the MPX area and it is because of the 
expected track of the upper low/Polo remnants.

Starting with the Montana shortwave, this is the one that 
will drive a cold front across the Dakotas tonight that will 
continue east across MN on Tuesday. We'll see rain showers spread 
into western early Tuesday morning, that will spread east with the 
front through the rest of the day. This boundary will push southeast 
of the MPX area Tuesday evening, taking the bulk of the rain with. 
The one thing to watch Tuesday night night is both the HRRR and RRFS 
are showing another widespread dense fog event unfolding across most 
of the MPX area behind this rain. In general, this is expected to 
bring a widespread 0.25" to 1" of rain to the area, with the highest 
amounts in south central and southeast MN. It's looking increasingly 
likely that this will be the extent of the precipitation we see in 
the Tuesday through Wednesday night time frame.

Now to the upper low and Hurricane Polo. These two features will 
merge Tuesday night over AZ/NM, with the remnant low ejecting out 
across the Plains toward the lower MO Valley by Thursday. This 
system will be filling in as it moves across the central CONUS, but 
the presence of remnant tropical moisture will push PWAT anomalies 
up toward the 300% of normal territory, but that moisture looks to 
only get as far north the cold front that pushes southeast of our 
area Tuesday night. After a drastic shift north yesterday with the 
GFS/GEFS in its QPF, we have seen the GFS settle back close to the 
QPF footprint the ECMWF-AIFS has basically had the last several 
days. This means confidence is now moderate to high that the heavy 
rain event for Wednesday/Wednesday night will remain south of the 
MPX area, with that heavy rain axis likely to line up from roughly 
the southwest corner of Iowa over to the IL/WI border. The northern 
edge of this rain shield may come up and clip the Albert Lea area on 
Wednesday, but it is looking increasingly likely that the threat for 
an excessive rainfall event in the MPX area this week has all but 
disappeared into Iowa.

Although the rain may miss us on Wednesday, it's not until Wednesday 
night that we see a legit cold frontal passage that will clear out 
the dewpoints in the 50s/60s and drop temperatures back. There is 
potential for a mild day, with highs into the low 70s on Wednesday, 
assuming we don't waste too much of the day trying to burn off 
another round of dense fog. Behind the cold front Wednesday night, 
we'll see lows fall back into the 30s with highs in the 60s. We'll 
see a clipper type system work across the international border on 
Saturday, but it will be moisture starved with the best forcing 
north of the MPX area. Still, you can't rule out a few showers 
moving through Saturday night before cool/dry Canadian high pressure 
moves in for Sunday to give us a dry end to the weekend. This will 
put in place perfect conditions on Sunday for those weirdos that 
think running 26.2 miles is a good idea (note, this is one of those 
weirdos). 

Early next week, the high from Sunday moves into the Great Lakes, 
with southerly flow quickly developing. This will bring in what is 
looking to be a milder (with respect to the ever falling normals) 
and drier stretch of weather. The drier part is good news for 
farmers looking to get a jump on the 2026 harvest.
